analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal paid family and medical leave insurance program paying workers up to twelve weeks of benefits.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 16, 2025 with 207 House cosponsors, all Democrats; referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would create a new federal insurance program, run by the Social Security Administration, that pays workers a monthly benefit while they take leave for a serious health condition, a new child, care for an ill or injured family member, or to recover from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Benefits replace 85% of earnings for lower-wage workers, 69% for middle earnings, and 50% above that, up to $4,000 a month and at least $580 a month. It covers self-employed people and workers of any employer, requires employers to give workers their job back and keep their health insurance during leave, and lets states that already run paid leave programs keep them with federal grants covering their costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who need time off for a new child, their own serious illness, care for a sick or dying family member, or safety from domestic or sexual violence — including self-employed, part-time, and low-wage workers who now have no paid leave. Most American workers have no paid family leave, and the program pays a share of wages during it.

how_it_helps.text: Workers can claim up to a full workweek of hours' worth of benefits per week, for up to about twelve weeks' worth of hours per year, for a serious health condition, a new child, care of a broad set of family members, or recovery from domestic or sexual violence [S2].

Benefits are steeply progressive: 85% of average monthly earnings up to $1,257, 69% of earnings up to $3,500, and 50% above that, with a monthly minimum of $580 and a maximum of $4,000 — so a low-wage caregiver replaces most of their pay while a high earner gets a capped amount [S2].

Eligibility is based on roughly $2,000 of wages or self-employment income over a recent 8-quarter window, so self-employed, part-time, and intermittent workers qualify, and workers who lost their jobs can still claim benefits for caregiving time already taken [S2].

Employers must restore workers to their same or an equivalent job after leave, keep group health coverage in force during leave, and face a presumption of illegal retaliation for any adverse action within 12 months of a leave, with damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees available in court [S2].

States that already run comprehensive paid leave programs (such as California, New York, and New Jersey) stay 'legacy states' and receive federal grants covering the cost of their programs and administration, with states able to pass a share through to employers and insurers providing the benefits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The bill routes benefits through a new Federal Family and Medical Leave Insurance Trust Fund; the financing mechanism is not included in the portion of the bill text provided. Employers bear direct compliance costs: they must hold jobs open, maintain health coverage during leave, and can be sued for retaliation with damages and fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, plus whoever funds the trust fund

drawbacks.text: The bill text establishes benefits payable from a new Federal Family and Medical Leave Insurance Trust Fund but the version provided does not state what funds it; comparable social-insurance programs are funded by dedicated payroll contributions, so workers and employers would face a new ongoing cost of that kind [S2].

Employers of every size must restore positions and maintain group health coverage during leave, and a rebuttable presumption of retaliation applies to any adverse personnel action within a year of leave — a compliance burden and litigation exposure that small businesses in particular would feel [S2].

Benefits can be reduced by workers' compensation or unemployment benefits an individual receives, and people already receiving disability benefits are ineligible, limiting the program for some claimants [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is large: a national guarantee of partial wage replacement during the moments — a birth, a cancer diagnosis, a dying parent — when workers today most often lose income or their job. The main honest objection is cost and design: a new entitlement with a financing mechanism not laid out in the text provided, plus real compliance burdens on employers, especially small ones. States that already run paid leave keep their own systems and get federal money for them, which preserves existing programs but makes the federal program one payer among several rather than the sole system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on September 16, 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the FAMILY Act in the House on September 16, 2025 [S1][S4].
It gathered 207 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S3].
The only action after introduction was referral to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over social-insurance programs [S4].
The committee has taken no further action; the bill sits there with the 119th Congress still in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill parked in committee, the status quo holds: workers who lack paid leave gain nothing yet, and employers face no new leave obligations or contributions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and workers with no paid leave

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAMILY Act and recruited 207 Democratic cosponsors on introduction day

for.name: 207 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Rep. Hoyer, and members from nearly every Democratic delegation
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the Social Security Administration, which would run the program
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has scheduled no hearing or markup; as of the record the committee has taken no action since September 16, 2025 [S4]

sides.party_line_note: All 207 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the committee that would act on it has a Republican majority [S3].

industries.note: Employers must restore workers to their jobs, maintain health coverage during leave, and face retaliation lawsuits with a 12-month presumption of retaliation; the bill text leaves the benefit financing mechanism unstated in the portion provided. Workers gain job-protected paid leave at employers' direct compliance expense.

industries.industry: State paid leave programs and the insurers/employers that provide benefits under them
industries.note: Legacy states (those with existing comprehensive paid leave laws) get federal grants covering their program and administration costs, and can pass shares of the grant through to employers and insurers providing benefits under state law. This locks in state programs and the private and multiemployer plans that deliver benefits under them.

Not an industry, but the bill's direct beneficiaries: self-employed, part-time, and low-wage workers currently have no federal paid family or medical leave and could claim progressive wage replacement while keeping their job and health coverage.

analysis.trajectory: This bill is at the earliest stage: referred to Ways and Means, with no markup scheduled and no Republican cosponsors. Most bills referred to committee in a divided government where the chamber's majority party does not support them never get a hearing or a vote, and this one is likely to sit until the Congress ends unless paid leave is attached to larger legislation.
